topic: the rise of Hitler and Nazi Germany

easy.text: Which political party did Adolf Hitler lead to power in Germany during the early 1930s?

options.feedback: Correct -- Hitler led the National Socialist German Workers' Party (Nazi Party) to power.
The Communist Party was actually a major rival that the Nazis suppressed, not the party Hitler led.
The Social Democrats were a mainstream Weimar-era party the Nazis opposed and later crushed, not Hitler's own party.
The Center Party was a separate Catholic-aligned Weimar-era party, not Hitler's own party.

medium.text: What event in early 1933 did the Nazi government use to justify suspending civil liberties and cracking down on political opponents?

options.feedback: Correct -- the fire at Germany's parliament building was used to justify emergency decrees suspending civil liberties.
The Beer Hall Putsch was Hitler's failed 1923 coup attempt, a decade earlier, not this 1933 event.
Kristallnacht was a later 1938 anti-Jewish pogrom, not this 1933 event.
The invasion of Poland came in 1939, starting World War II, well after this 1933 event.

hard.text: Which 1933 law effectively allowed Hitler's government to bypass parliament and rule by decree, cementing dictatorial power?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Enabling Act let Hitler's cabinet enact laws without the Reichstag's approval, effectively establishing dictatorship.
The Treaty of Versailles was the 1919 peace treaty imposed on Germany after World War I, not a Nazi-era power grab.
The Nuremberg Laws were 1935 racial laws, distinct from this 1933 act concerning parliamentary power.
This was a 1939 non-aggression pact between Germany and the Soviet Union, unrelated to domestic parliamentary power.

easy.easy: This party's full name is often shortened to the initials NSDAP.
easy.medium: This is the party whose leader became German chancellor in 1933.
easy.hard: Distinguish this from Germany's other Weimar-era parties -- this is the specific movement Hitler himself led.

medium.medium: This is not the failed 1923 coup attempt, nor the 1938 anti-Jewish violence, nor the 1939 invasion that started WWII.
medium.hard: This specific 1933 building fire is distinct from Hitler's earlier failed putsch, the later Kristallnacht pogrom, and the still-later invasion of Poland.

hard.easy: This law's name suggests granting extraordinary power to the government.
hard.medium: This is not the WWI peace treaty, the later racial laws, or the later pact with the Soviet Union.
hard.hard: This 1933 law is distinct from the earlier Versailles treaty, the later Nuremberg racial laws, and the later Nazi-Soviet non-aggression pact -- it's specifically what let Hitler rule without parliament.

easy.text: The Spanish Civil War (1936-1939) was fought between the Republican government and Nationalist forces led by which general?

options.feedback: Correct -- Franco led the Nationalist forces and ruled Spain as dictator after their victory.
Mussolini's Italy supported Franco's Nationalists, but Mussolini himself was an Italian leader, not the Spanish general leading them.
Hitler's Germany supported Franco's Nationalists, but Hitler was a German leader, not the Spanish general leading them.

options.text: The United States and United Kingdom

options.text: Imperial Japan and the Ottoman Empire
options.feedback: The Ottoman Empire no longer existed by this time, and Japan was not a direct supporter of Franco's forces.

hard.text: The 1937 bombing of which Spanish town, carried out by Germany's Condor Legion in support of Franco, became infamous and inspired a famous Picasso painting?

options.feedback: Correct -- the bombing of Guernica became a global symbol of civilian wartime suffering, memorialized in Picasso's painting of the same name.
Madrid, Spain's capital, was besieged during the war, but it is not the town whose bombing inspired Picasso's famous painting.
Barcelona was a major Republican stronghold, but it is not the town whose bombing inspired Picasso's famous painting.
Toledo saw fighting during the war, but it is not the town whose bombing inspired Picasso's famous painting.

easy.medium: This is not the Italian or German dictator who supported him, nor the later Yugoslav leader.
easy.hard: Distinguish the Spanish general who actually led the Nationalists from his foreign fascist supporters and unrelated leaders elsewhere in Europe.

medium.medium: The other pair of countries listed actually supported the opposing Republican side or stayed uninvolved.
medium.hard: The two true supporters were the era's major fascist powers, distinct from the Western democracies (largely neutral) and the Soviet Union/Mexico (which backed the Republicans instead).

hard.medium: This is not Spain's capital or its largest coastal city, nor a historic city famous for its medieval architecture -- it's a smaller Basque town.

topic: the Dust Bowl and the New Deal

easy.text: Which two conditions combined to cause the severe dust storms of the 1930s 'Dust Bowl' on the American Great Plains? (Select all that apply)

options.feedback: Correct -- years of extreme drought dried out the soil across the Great Plains.

options.text: Farming practices that stripped away protective native grasses
options.feedback: Correct -- deep plowing removed the grasses that had held the topsoil in place.
The Dust Bowl was caused by a lack of rain, not excessive rainfall or flooding.
No volcanic eruption caused the Dust Bowl -- drought and poor farming practices were the causes.

medium.text: Which two New Deal programs, created under President Franklin D. Roosevelt, aimed to provide jobs and address the economic crisis of the 1930s? (Select all that apply)

options.feedback: Correct -- the CCC put young unemployed men to work on conservation and public works projects.
Correct -- the WPA employed millions on public infrastructure and arts projects during the Depression.
The Marshall Plan was a later, post-World War II program to rebuild Europe, not a domestic New Deal program.
The Federal Reserve was created decades earlier, in 1913, not as part of the New Deal.

hard.text: Which two outcomes resulted from the combination of the Dust Bowl and the Great Depression in the 1930s? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Large-scale migration of displaced farming families, especially to California
options.feedback: Correct -- many families, often called 'Okies,' migrated west seeking work after losing their farms.

options.text: New federal conservation programs aimed at preventing future soil erosion
options.feedback: Correct -- the crisis prompted new federal efforts like the Soil Conservation Service.

options.text: A sharp increase in immigration into the affected Great Plains states
options.feedback: The Plains states saw people leaving in large numbers, not new immigration arriving.

options.text: A boom in agricultural land prices across the Great Plains
options.feedback: Land values fell sharply during this crisis, rather than booming.

easy.easy: Both correct causes date to the 1930s Plains: one is simply a long run of very dry weather, and the other is deep plowing that left the soil bare without its natural grass cover -- it wasn't flooding or a volcano.
easy.medium: Think dry conditions plus soil left exposed by farming, not the opposite of either.
easy.hard: One cause is about weather; the other is about how the land had been farmed beforehand.

medium.easy: Both correct programs put unemployed Americans to work on public projects during the Depression.
medium.medium: One later program helped rebuild Europe after WWII, and the other is a much older banking institution -- neither belongs here.
medium.hard: The two true programs are Depression-era job-creation agencies, distinct from a later European recovery plan and a much earlier banking system reform.

hard.easy: Both true outcomes followed directly from the crisis: many farm families packed up and headed west for work, and the government launched new programs to stop the soil erosion from happening again.
hard.medium: This period saw people leaving the Plains, not new arrivals, and falling farm values, not rising ones.
hard.hard: One outcome involves people leaving the region; the other involves the government trying to prevent a repeat.

easy.text: The Holocaust refers to Nazi Germany's systematic genocide during World War II, targeting primarily which group?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Holocaust was the Nazi regime's systematic genocide of six million European Jews, along with other targeted groups.
Political prisoners were among those persecuted, but the Holocaust's primary and defining target was Europe's Jewish population.
Soviet POWs suffered terribly under Nazi rule, but the Holocaust specifically refers to the genocide targeting Jewish people.
French citizens as a nationality were not the Holocaust's defining target -- Jewish people across all of occupied Europe were.

medium.text: What term did the Nazi regime use for its plan to systematically exterminate European Jews, formalized at the 1942 Wannsee Conference?

options.feedback: Correct -- 'the Final Solution' was the Nazi regime's own chilling term for its genocidal extermination plan.
The Marshall Plan was an unrelated postwar economic recovery program for Europe.
Lebensraum referred to Nazi ideology about territorial expansion, distinct from this specific extermination plan's name.
Blitzkrieg was a military tactic of rapid, coordinated attack, not the name of the genocidal plan.

hard.text: Which camp is most widely recognized as the largest Nazi extermination and concentration camp complex, where the greatest number of Holocaust victims were killed?

options.feedback: Correct -- Auschwitz-Birkenau, in occupied Poland, was the largest and deadliest of the Nazi camps.
Dachau was an earlier camp primarily used for political prisoners within Germany, not the largest extermination site.
Buchenwald was a major concentration camp in Germany, but not the largest extermination complex.
Bergen-Belsen was a significant camp, but not the largest extermination complex -- that was Auschwitz-Birkenau.

easy.easy: This group faced the Nazi regime's most extensive and systematic campaign of extermination, though other groups were also targeted.
easy.medium: This is the primary group defined by their religion and ethnicity, targeted continent-wide, not a single nationality or POW group.
easy.hard: Distinguish the primary targeted group -- defined by religion and ethnicity across many countries -- from narrower groups like one nation's POWs or citizens.

medium.easy: This term is the regime's own chilling euphemism for its extermination plan.
medium.medium: This isn't a military tactic or an expansionist territorial ideology, nor a postwar recovery plan -- it's the specific genocidal policy name.
medium.hard: This is the plan's own formal internal name, distinct from the military blitz tactic, the territorial expansion ideology, and an unrelated postwar economic plan.

hard.easy: This camp complex, in occupied Poland, is the single deadliest of all the camps.
hard.medium: This is not one of the earlier, primarily political-prisoner camps in Germany itself.
hard.hard: This is specifically the largest extermination complex by death toll, distinct from earlier concentration camps within Germany that held mostly political prisoners.

easy.text: The Battle of Stalingrad (1942-1943) was a major turning point on which front of World War II?

options.text: The Eastern Front, between Germany and the Soviet Union
options.feedback: Correct -- Stalingrad was fought deep in Soviet territory on the Eastern Front.

options.text: The Pacific theater, between the U.S. and Japan
options.feedback: The Pacific theater was a separate front against Japan, not where Stalingrad was fought.
North Africa was a separate campaign, not the location of the Stalingrad battle.
The Western Front in France was a separate theater, not the location of the Stalingrad battle.

medium.text: Which side ultimately won the Battle of Stalingrad, marking a major shift in momentum in the war against Nazi Germany?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Soviet Red Army encircled and defeated German forces at Stalingrad.
Germany suffered a devastating defeat at Stalingrad -- the Soviets won.
The UK was not a direct combatant in this specific battle -- it was fought between Germany and the Soviet Union.
The U.S. was not a direct combatant in this specific battle -- it was fought between Germany and the Soviet Union.

hard.text: Which German commander's surrender of his encircled army at Stalingrad in early 1943 marked the first time a German field marshal had surrendered?

options.feedback: Correct -- Paulus surrendered his trapped Sixth Army, becoming the first German field marshal to do so.
Rommel is famous for commanding German forces in North Africa, not the surrender at Stalingrad.
Guderian was a renowned German tank commander, not the officer who surrendered at Stalingrad.
Keitel signed Germany's overall surrender in 1945, a separate and later event from Paulus's surrender at Stalingrad.

easy.text: The D-Day invasion of June 6, 1944, was a massive Allied invasion of Nazi-occupied territory in which country?

Montgomery commanded British ground forces, but he served under Eisenhower's overall command, not as supreme commander.
MacArthur commanded in the Pacific theater, not the European invasion.

easy.text: The Battle of Midway (1942) was a major turning point in which theater of World War II?

options.feedback: Correct -- Midway was a decisive naval battle in the Pacific theater against Japan.
The Eastern Front was fought between Germany and the Soviet Union, an entirely separate theater.
North Africa was a separate campaign, not the location of the Midway battle.

options.feedback: Correct -- American cryptographers had broken key Japanese naval codes, revealing Japan's attack plans in advance.
The U.S. actually had fewer carriers than Japan at Midway -- the real advantage was intelligence, not numbers.
The Soviet Union was not involved in this Pacific naval battle.
Midway was primarily a naval and air battle, not decided by a land invasion force.

hard.text: How many Japanese aircraft carriers were sunk during the Battle of Midway, a devastating loss for Japan's naval air power?

options.feedback: Correct -- Japan lost four fleet carriers at Midway, a crippling blow it never fully recovered from.
Japan's losses were far greater than just one carrier -- four were sunk.

topic: the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki

easy.text: In August 1945, the United States dropped atomic bombs on two Japanese cities. Name one of these two cities.

options.feedback: Correct -- Hiroshima, along with Nagasaki, was struck by an atomic bomb in August 1945.
Tokyo, Japan's capital, was heavily bombed conventionally, but it was not one of the two atomic bomb targets.
Kyoto was actually removed from the target list and spared, not one of the two cities struck.
Osaka was not one of the two cities struck by atomic bombs.

medium.text: What was the immediate broader consequence of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki?

options.text: Japan's surrender, ending World War II
options.feedback: Correct -- Japan surrendered shortly after the bombings, bringing World War II to a close.

options.text: The start of the Korean War
options.feedback: The Korean War began years later, in 1950, not as an immediate consequence of the bombings.

options.text: The founding of the United Nations
options.feedback: The United Nations was established through a separate diplomatic process around this time, not as a direct consequence of the bombings.

options.text: Japan's invasion of the Soviet Union

hard.text: How many days apart were the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki?

The gap was much shorter -- just three days, not months.

easy.text: Which two Allied leaders, along with Joseph Stalin, made up the 'Big Three' who met at the Yalta Conference in February 1945? (Select all that apply)

options.feedback: Correct -- Roosevelt represented the United States at Yalta.
Correct -- Churchill represented the United Kingdom at Yalta.
De Gaulle led Free France, but France was not among the 'Big Three' at Yalta.
Truman became U.S. president only after Roosevelt's death in April 1945, after the Yalta Conference had already occurred.

medium.text: Which two topics were major agenda items discussed at the Yalta Conference? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Dividing postwar Germany into occupation zones
options.feedback: Correct -- the leaders discussed how to divide and administer defeated Germany.

options.text: Soviet entry into the war against Japan
options.feedback: Correct -- Stalin agreed at Yalta to eventually join the war against Japan.

options.text: The immediate establishment of the Marshall Plan for European recovery
options.feedback: The Marshall Plan was a separate U.S. economic recovery program announced in 1947, two years after the Yalta Conference -- it was not agreed at Yalta.

options.text: The final negotiation of Japan's unconditional surrender terms
options.feedback: Japan's actual surrender terms were hammered out later in 1945, after Yalta -- the conference itself only secured Stalin's promise to eventually join the Pacific war.

hard.text: Which two of the following are accurate about the Yalta Conference's outcomes and setting? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It was held in Crimea, within Soviet territory
options.feedback: Correct -- the conference took place in Yalta, on the Crimean peninsula.

options.text: It laid groundwork for the postwar United Nations organization
options.feedback: Correct -- the leaders discussed plans for a new international organization that became the United Nations.

options.text: It formally ended World War II
options.feedback: The war continued for several more months after the conference -- it did not formally end the war.

options.text: It resulted in Germany's unconditional surrender being signed on-site
options.feedback: Germany's surrender was signed months later, elsewhere, not at the Yalta Conference itself.

easy.easy: The two correct 'Big Three' members alongside Stalin are the U.S. and British wartime leaders -- not France's leader or Roosevelt's eventual successor.
easy.medium: Neither correct leader is the French general who led the Free French, nor the man who became president only after this conference.
easy.hard: One leader was the sitting American president at the time; the other was Britain's wartime prime minister.

medium.medium: Neither correct topic is the 1947 U.S. aid initiative for Europe or the eventual negotiated end to the Pacific war.
medium.hard: One topic concerns dividing a defeated nation; the other concerns bringing a new Allied power into the Pacific war.

hard.medium: The war itself continued for months afterward, and Germany's surrender was signed elsewhere, later.
hard.hard: One truth is about the conference's location; the other is about a later international organization it helped set up.

easy.text: After World War II, major Nazi leaders were prosecuted for war crimes in a series of trials held in which German city?

options.feedback: Correct -- the trials were held in Nuremberg, giving them their name.

medium.text: The Nuremberg Trials were conducted by an international tribunal representing which four Allied powers?

options.text: The United States, the United Kingdom, the Soviet Union, and France

options.text: The United States, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand

hard.text: The Nuremberg Trials are historically significant for establishing what precedent in international law?

options.text: That individuals, including state and military officials, can be held personally criminally accountable for war crimes and crimes against humanity
options.feedback: Correct -- Nuremberg established that individuals, not just nations, bear personal legal responsibility for atrocities.

options.text: That nations can never be held responsible for wartime actions

options.text: That international law only applies to civilians, not soldiers

options.text: That war crimes trials can only be conducted by the country whose citizens committed them

easy.medium: This is not Germany's capital, nor the city associated with the earlier Beer Hall Putsch, nor a major northern port city.

hard.hard: This legal precedent concerns who can ultimately be held responsible, and on what basis -- rule out the ideas that nations alone bear responsibility, that only civilians are covered, or that a country can only try its own citizens.

hard.medium: This isn't a U.S. hemispheric policy or a broader doctrine of aid to threatened nations -- it's the treaty's own specific numbered article.

easy.text: Which two facts accurately describe the Warsaw Pact, founded in 1955? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It was a collective defense alliance led by the Soviet Union
options.feedback: Correct -- the Soviet Union led this Eastern Bloc defense alliance.

options.text: It included Eastern Bloc communist states such as Poland and East Germany
options.feedback: Correct -- member states included Poland, East Germany, and other Soviet-aligned nations.
NATO was founded in 1949, six years before the Warsaw Pact was established in 1955.

options.text: It included the United States as a member
options.feedback: The United States was a NATO member and Cold War rival, not part of the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact.

medium.text: Which two factors are commonly cited as prompting the Soviet Union to establish the Warsaw Pact? (Select all that apply)

options.text: A desire to formally counterbalance NATO
options.feedback: Correct -- the Warsaw Pact was created partly as a direct counterweight to NATO.

options.text: West Germany's admission into NATO that same year
options.feedback: Correct -- West Germany joining NATO in 1955 was a direct trigger for the Warsaw Pact's formation.

options.text: A joint declaration of war against the United States
options.feedback: The Warsaw Pact was a defensive alliance structure, not a declaration of war against the U.S.

options.text: A merger with the League of Nations
options.feedback: The League of Nations had already dissolved years earlier and played no role in the Warsaw Pact's founding.

hard.text: Which two of the following accurately describe the Warsaw Pact's eventual end? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It was formally dissolved in 1991, coinciding with the end of the Cold War
options.feedback: Correct -- the Warsaw Pact was formally dissolved in 1991 as the Cold War ended.

options.text: Its dissolution followed the collapse of Soviet-aligned communist governments in Eastern Europe
options.feedback: Correct -- the fall of communist governments across Eastern Europe preceded the Pact's dissolution.

options.text: It remains active today under a different name
options.feedback: The Warsaw Pact does not exist today under any name -- it was fully dissolved in 1991.

options.text: It was replaced immediately by a merger with NATO
options.feedback: There was no merger with NATO -- the Warsaw Pact simply dissolved as its member states' communist governments fell.

easy.easy: The two truths are Soviet leadership and membership of Eastern European communist states -- ruling out an earlier founding date than NATO or U.S. membership.
easy.medium: This alliance came after, not before, its Western counterpart, and it didn't include any Western powers.
easy.hard: One truth is about leadership; the other is about which nations belonged to it.

medium.easy: The two real factors are direct responses to NATO's existence and West Germany's admission into it that year -- not a declaration of war or an unrelated merger.
medium.medium: Neither factor involves a declared war on the U.S. or a merger with an older international body.
medium.hard: One factor is about matching a rival alliance; the other is about a specific country joining that rival alliance.

hard.easy: The two accurate facts are its 1991 dissolution and that this followed Eastern Europe's communist governments collapsing -- not ongoing existence or a NATO merger.
hard.medium: This alliance did not survive to today under any name, and it wasn't absorbed into NATO.
hard.hard: One truth is about timing; the other is about what caused that timing.

topic: the Chinese Civil War and the rise of Mao Zedong

easy.text: The Chinese Civil War was fought primarily between the Communist Party of China and which rival political-military force?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Communists fought the Nationalist Party, led by Chiang Kai-shek, for control of China.
Japan was a common wartime enemy during part of this period, but the civil war itself was fought against a rival Chinese faction.
The Soviet Union supported the Communists at times, but it was not the rival force fought in the civil war itself.
The Ottoman Empire had no involvement in the Chinese Civil War.

medium.text: Who led the Communist forces to final victory in the Chinese Civil War in 1949?

options.feedback: Correct -- Mao led the Communist Party to victory and proclaimed the People's Republic of China in 1949.
Chiang Kai-shek led the defeated Nationalist forces, not the victorious Communists.
Deng Xiaoping rose to lead China decades later, after Mao's era, not during the civil war's conclusion.
Sun Yat-sen was an earlier Chinese revolutionary figure who died in 1925, before this civil war's decisive phase.

hard.text: After their defeat in the Chinese Civil War, where did the Nationalist government under Chiang Kai-shek relocate to continue governing?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Nationalists retreated to the island of Taiwan, where they continued to govern the Republic of China.
Hong Kong was a separate British colonial territory, not where the Nationalist government relocated.
Vietnam was a separate Southeast Asian country, not where the Nationalist government relocated.
The Philippines was a separate country, not where the Nationalist government relocated.

easy.easy: This rival force was led by a general who also fought against Japanese occupation earlier.
easy.medium: This is a Chinese domestic political rival, not a foreign occupying power or another nation entirely.
easy.hard: Distinguish the Communists' actual Chinese civil-war rival from Japan (a separate wartime enemy) or unrelated foreign powers.

medium.easy: This leader proclaimed a new communist state in China in October 1949.
medium.medium: This is not the defeated Nationalist leader, nor a Chinese leader who rose to power decades later, nor an earlier revolutionary who died before this war's key battles.
medium.hard: Distinguish the victorious Communist leader from his defeated Nationalist rival, from China's later post-Mao leader, and from an earlier revolutionary figure who predates this conflict.

hard.easy: This location is an island off China's coast, where the defeated government continued to exist separately.
hard.medium: This is not a British colonial territory, nor a Southeast Asian mainland nation.
hard.hard: The Nationalists' retreat was specifically to this island, distinct from Hong Kong's separate colonial status or any Southeast Asian mainland country.

easy.text: The Great Leap Forward, launched by Mao Zedong in the late 1950s, aimed to rapidly transform China through what kind of changes?

options.feedback: Correct -- the campaign pushed for rapid industrial output and collectivized farming across China.
The Great Leap Forward pushed further toward state-controlled collectivization, not democratization or free markets.

options.text: Rapid religious conversion of the population
options.feedback: Religious conversion was not the campaign's goal -- economic and agricultural transformation was.
The campaign was a domestic economic and agricultural program, not a war of territorial expansion.

medium.text: The Great Leap Forward is most infamously associated with contributing to which catastrophic outcome?

options.text: A massive famine that killed tens of millions of people
options.feedback: Correct -- the campaign's failed policies contributed to one of history's deadliest famines.

options.text: A rapid economic boom with no negative consequences
options.feedback: The campaign was actually a catastrophic failure, not a boom without negative consequences.
Taiwan was not reunified with mainland China during or after this campaign.

options.text: A sharp decline in China's population growth due to strict new birth-control laws
options.feedback: This describes the later, separate one-child policy, not the Great Leap Forward's famine-driven catastrophe.

hard.text: Which specific, now-notorious practice during the Great Leap Forward -- encouraging households to melt down metal in small home furnaces -- exemplified the campaign's disastrous approach to rapid industrialization?

options.feedback: Correct -- households were pushed to produce steel in crude backyard furnaces, largely yielding unusable metal.
The Bessemer process was an actual efficient 19th-century industrial steelmaking method, unrelated to this crude home-furnace campaign.
The assembly line is a modern factory production technique, not this crude home-based method.
Collective farming was a real feature of the era, but the specific home-furnace steel campaign described here is distinct from farming cooperatives.

easy.easy: This campaign pushed both farming and industry to change dramatically and quickly, in a communist direction, not a free-market one.
easy.medium: This wasn't about religion or military conquest -- it was an economic and agricultural transformation.
easy.hard: This concerns what kind of sweeping change Mao's campaign pursued -- rule out political liberalization toward free markets, religious transformation, and territorial conquest through war, and consider what a communist state under continued central control would still be pushing hard to change.

medium.easy: The outcome was devastating rather than positive, and unrelated to Taiwan or birth-control policy.
medium.medium: This is not the later one-child policy's demographic effects, nor a peaceful cross-strait reunification -- it was a food crisis.
medium.hard: The real outcome was a catastrophic human tragedy caused by the campaign's failed policies, distinct from a later, separate birth-control program or any peaceful reunification with Taiwan.

hard.easy: This practice involved ordinary households trying to produce metal at home using crude methods.
hard.medium: This is not an efficient 19th-century industrial process or a modern factory technique -- it's a crude, small-scale home method that largely failed to produce usable metal.
hard.hard: Rule out the genuinely efficient 19th-century industrial steelmaking method, the modern factory-based production system, and the era's separate rural collectivization program -- eliminating those three by what you know of their real nature leaves only the specific practice the question itself is asking you to name.
